objective: Học xong bài này, bạn sẽ xác định được ý chính của từng đoạn trước khi chọn tiêu đề, và phân biệt thông tin bài nêu rõ với thông tin bài không hề nhắc tới, trong bài đọc về thiết kế bệnh viện hỗ trợ hồi phục.

sentences.text: For most of the twentieth century, hospitals were designed above all for the efficient movement of doctors, nurses and equipment.
Long corridors connected wards, operating theatres and laboratories, while patients were expected to fit quietly into a system organised around the working routines of staff.
Whether patients could see daylight, sleep without interruption or find their own way to an appointment was treated as a minor detail.
In recent decades, however, researchers have begun to ask a different question: whether the building itself can influence how quickly people recover.
The evidence collected so far suggests that it can, and architects now talk of healing environments, buildings designed to support recovery rather than merely to house treatment.
What began as a question in research journals has now become a standard item on the brief given to hospital architects.
One of the most frequently cited studies in this field compared two groups of patients recovering from the same operation in the same hospital.
Patients in rooms facing a small group of trees left hospital sooner and requested less strong pain relief than patients whose windows faced a plain brick wall.
The two groups were alike in age and in the care they received, so the researchers concluded that the view itself contributed to the difference.
Other studies have linked generous daylight to better sleep, steadier mood and lower levels of tiredness among patients during their stay.
As a result, new hospital wards are often arranged so that beds receive natural light for much of the day, and many designs place gardens where patients can see them from their windows.
Noise is a second feature of the traditional hospital that designers are now trying to change.
Measurements taken on busy wards have recorded regular peaks from alarms, metal trolleys, telephones and conversations at the nursing station, sometimes continuing throughout the night.
Such noise repeatedly interrupts sleep, and poor sleep is not a minor discomfort for someone recovering from surgery or serious illness.
Sleep is when the body repairs tissue and fights infection, so a patient who is woken every hour is likely to heal more slowly.
Designers have responded with single rooms, sound-absorbing ceiling materials and quieter equipment, all intended to protect the rest of patients.
In one pilot project, simply moving the nursing station away from the ward entrance reduced night-time noise noticeably and improved the sleep quality that patients reported.
The layout of a hospital can also raise or lower stress for the people who use it every day.
Visitors who get lost in identical corridors arrive at the ward anxious and late, and nurses lose valuable time giving directions instead of providing care.
Clear sightlines, colour-coded routes and views to the outside all help people to orient themselves without needing to ask for help.
Patients, meanwhile, feel less helpless when they can adjust their own lighting, open a window or choose when relatives visit them.
This sense of control matters because a long stay can make patients feel that everything about their day is decided for them.
Family spaces, small gardens and quiet rooms for private conversations are now treated as part of treatment itself rather than decoration.
Even the position of a handrail or the colour of a door can make a ward feel calmer or more confusing.
Healing design is not cheap, since single rooms, larger windows and planted courtyards all raise the cost of construction considerably.
Supporters argue that the extra expense is recovered when patients leave earlier and fewer complications occur, although such savings are difficult to prove precisely.
Critics also point out that for some features the evidence remains thin, resting on small studies carried out in a single hospital.
Nevertheless, the direction of travel is clear, and few new hospitals are now built without considering light, noise and layout as clinical issues.
The building, in other words, has joined medicines and surgery as something that can either support recovery or stand in its way.

evidence.quote: Patients in rooms facing a small group of trees left hospital sooner and requested less strong pain relief than patients whose windows faced a plain brick wall.

explanation.trap: Câu hỏi đổi 'requested' thành 'asked for' và 'less strong' thành 'less powerful'; hai cách diễn đạt tương đương nên đáp án vẫn là TRUE.
explanation.whyCorrect: Đoạn B nói nhóm bệnh nhân ở phòng hướng ra cây xin thuốc giảm đau nhẹ hơn nhóm nhìn ra bức tường gạch trơn.
explanation.whyWrong: Không phải NOT GIVEN vì bài khẳng định trực tiếp bằng cụm 'requested less strong pain relief' trong câu so sánh hai nhóm.

questions.stem: Patients whose windows faced trees asked for less powerful pain relief than patients whose windows faced a wall.

explanation.trap: Người đọc tự điền con số vào khoảng trống của bài là bẫy NOT GIVEN kinh điển; 'sooner' không đồng nghĩa với bất kỳ con số cụ thể nào.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bài nói nhóm hướng ra cây 'left hospital sooner' nhưng không hề định lượng sớm hơn bao nhiêu ngày, nên con số hai ngày không có cơ sở trong bài.
explanation.whyWrong: Không phải TRUE vì số ngày không xuất hiện. Không phải FALSE vì bài cũng không phủ nhận con số đó, bài chỉ im lặng về thời lượng.

nearMiss.quote: Patients in rooms facing a small group of trees left hospital sooner and requested less strong pain relief than patients whose windows faced a plain brick wall.
nearMiss.whyNotEnough: Bài chỉ nói nhóm nhìn ra cây ra viện sớm hơn, không cho con số ngày cụ thể nào cho cả hai nhóm.

notGivenProof.result: Không câu nào trong bài cho số ngày nằm viện cụ thể của bất kỳ nhóm bệnh nhân nào.

sentences.text: Hospitals never truly close, but some now try to behave as if they do after nine in the evening.
Under quiet-hours policies, staff dim corridor lights, silence non-urgent alarms and postpone routine observations until morning where it is safe to do so.
The aim is to protect the hours when patients are most likely to sleep deeply and wake least often.
Early results from hospitals that have adopted the policy suggest that patients report better rest and request fewer sleeping tablets than before.
Nurses, however, must balance quiet against safety, because some checks cannot be delayed without putting patients at risk.
Some hospitals have extended the idea to the early morning, delaying non-urgent blood tests until patients have had a full night of sleep.
The policy has also changed how wards are organised during the night shift.
Medicines that are due during the night are prepared in advance, and noisy equipment such as floor-cleaning machines is kept away from sleeping areas until morning.
Visitors are asked to leave earlier than they once did, although exceptions are made for relatives of seriously ill patients.
Managers say the changes cost little, since they depend mainly on reorganising routines rather than buying equipment.
Whether quieter nights actually shorten stays is still being studied, but staff already report calmer wards after dark.
Families of patients have generally welcomed the calmer evenings, although a few visitors complain that the shorter visiting time feels rushed.
The policy is reviewed each winter to check that safety has not suffered.
